item.title: TD, BMO named in U.S. debanking investigation report
item.description: A U.S. banking regulator has identified Bank of Montreal and TD Bank, along with seven other lenders, in a report about debanking and limiting access to financial services for certain U.S. customers ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: A U.S. banking regulator has identified Bank of Montreal and TD Bank, along with seven other lenders, in a report about debanking and limiting access to financial services for certain U.S. customers due to their political beliefs. The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released a report based on findings from a supervisory review of debanking activities at nine of the largest banks it oversees, based on 100,000 complaints at OCC-regulated institutions. The OCC says its review was conducted after an executive order by U.S. President Donald Trump, signed in August of last year, stipulating that Americans should not be denied access to financial services due to religious or political beliefs. Jonathan Gould, the comptroller of the currency, says the named banks “denied, debanked and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses.” TD did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while BMO referred The Canadian Press to a statement from the Bank Policy Institute. The institute, a U.S. industry advocacy group, says that it supports fair access to banking services and has been “working to ensure that government regulations and policies enable banks to serve law-abiding customers.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026. Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

item.title: U.S. stocks drop to their worst day since July as inflation worsens
item.description: NEW YORK — Worries about worsening inflation are dragging the U.S. stock market toward its worst day since June.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — U.S. stocks dropped to their worst day since July on Wednesday following the latest signal that inflation is getting worse. The S&P 500 sank 1.1 per cent for a fifth loss in the six days since setting its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 48 points, or 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slid 1.9 per cent as stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led the way lower. Stocks felt pressure from rising yields in the bond market, where worries grew after a report said U.S. consumers had to pay prices for fuel, food and other costs of living last month that were 3.7 per cent higher overall than a year earlier. That means inflation accelerated from its 3.4 per cent rate in August and was worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected. Inflation has remained more painful than anyone would like since the economy catapulted out of the crevasse created by the COVID-19 pandemic. It’s accelerated recently in part because of jumps in fuel prices caused by the war with Iran, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude added 0.4 per cent Wednesday to US$106.06. That has added to the longstanding worries about fast-rising debt loads for governments, signals that the U.S. economy is still growing and other factors that have sent bond yields to their highest levels in years. The centerpiece of the U.S. bond market, the 10-year Treasury, saw its yield briefly jump above 5.32 per cent from less than 5.17 per cent just before the inflation report’s release. It eventually gave back much of the gain. Yields on shorter-term Treasurys had even bigger leaps as traders raised their expectations for coming hikes to interest rates by the Federal Reserve, though they also moderated as the day progressed. The Fed recently raised the interest rate that it controls, which affects very short-term loans, for the first time in three years in hopes of reining in inflation. Higher rates do that by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and slowing the overall economy. Traders now see a nearly 35 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its next meeting in two weeks, up from the 22 per cent probability seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. Part of what’s keeping inflation high is that Americans overall are continuing to spend, which encourages businesses to keep raising prices for their products and services. As Americans become more “price-sensitive” and the economy also benefits from greater productivity by workers, Vanguard Senior Economist Adam Schickling said inflation should slow, but “patience will be required.” Much of Wall Street’s pain on Wednesday was due to drops for companies riding the AI frenzy to huge profit growth and stellar stock gains. Higher bond yields making borrowing money more expensive could make it more difficult for companies to raise cash to build data centers and fill them with AI chips. Drops of 3.2 per cent for Nvidia, 3.1 per cent for Broadcom and 5.7 per cent for Advanced Micro Devices were among the day’s heaviest weights on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, tumbled 15.5 per cent for its worst day since February. GE Vernova, which is hoping to electrify power-hungry data centers, dropped 6.2 per cent, and Oracle sank 8.8 per cent. Smaller companies also feel the bite of higher interest rates because many need to borrow to grow. The Russell 2000 index of the smallest U.S. stocks fell 1.9 per cent. Higher yields in the bond market push downward on prices for all kinds of stocks, and the main way companies can offset that is by delivering bigger profits. That’s exactly what analysts are expecting, and it’s how the S&P 500 has been able to set records despite the many challenges weighing on Wall Street. But the high expectations also mean companies will likely get punished if they fall short of targets for growth. Bank of America dropped 4.8 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the summer than analysts expected. The profit would have failed to meet expectations even if the U.S. Treasury Department had not announced US$1.2 billion in fines late Tuesday for alleged violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws by the bank. State Street sank 4.1 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though its profit was slightly above their forecasts. All told, the S&P 500 fell 86.51 points to 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 48.62 to 51,621.48, and the Nasdaq composite sank 511.51 to 26,692.87. In stock markets abroad, indexes ticked higher in Europe following a weaker finish in Asia. They rose 0.7 per cent in London and fell 0.9 per cent in Shanghai for two of the world’s bigger moves. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

item.title: Hot Picks: Three U.S. airline stocks to watch as fuel costs rise
item.description: Explore the investment case for Delta, United and Southwest as higher fuel costs put pressure on U.S. airline earnings.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Higher fuel prices are putting pressure on airline earnings, sharpening the focus on which carriers can withstand a tougher operating environment. Financial resilience is central to the investment case for the sector. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Atul Maheswari, equity analyst at UBS, about why he favours Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines and how he assesses their prospects. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: ANDREW: Our guest focuses on the airline sector and has three companies to put on your radar. Let’s bring in Atul Maheswari, equity analyst at UBS. Thank you very much indeed for joining us. ATUL: Thank you for having me as well. ANDREW: Start off with Delta, if you would. The company just warned investors about the impact of higher fuel prices, but you reckon the stock is attractive right now? ATUL: I think so. And look, I mean, fuel is basically — it is what it is right now. But, you know, Delta has been one of the better-positioned airlines because of the premium exposure that they have. They’ve been on this premiumization journey for over a decade. That’s continuing to — that’s continuing to yield good results for Delta. And, you know, there is volatility right now with respect to earnings because of what fuel is doing. But really, if you look at how Delta has performed over the last few years, even in a tough operating environment, they’re still generating decent margins. They’re still generating a lot of cash flow, and the balance sheet is very strong. So, you know, on the other side of this, whenever fuel does moderate, we would expect this company to perform pretty well on both the top line as well as on the bottom line. ANDREW: And so, you touch on this. They’re still loading up the planes even after increasing prices. ATUL: They’re still loading up the planes. Their load factors, which is the percentage of planes that is — that is full, was up year over year, even in an environment wherein fares have moved up significantly. So that goes to show that, you know, consumers are still flying with Delta, even as, you know, fares have gone up. ANDREW: United Airlines has a diversified stream of revenue, and that’s the reason you like the stock. Can you explain how do they have this big business mix? ATUL: So, you know, both Delta and United, you know, with respect to the diversified business mix, they have a large portion of the business that’s coming from the front of the cabin, so the premium as well as the premium economy or the Premium Plus seating. Also, a good portion of revenues come from loyalty. There is also cargo in the mix, and in the case of Delta, there’s also MRO in the mix. So there’s this more widely diversified revenue base, as opposed to relying only on a single cabin and a single revenue stream. Another important business segment to keep in mind, in the case of United, but also for Delta, is that business travel’s a larger portion for both these enterprises, and business travel has been particularly strong. So having this diversified revenue mix helps them, you know, better manage business volatility during tougher times. ANDREW: And Southwest Airlines, a model for so many discount airlines, what do you — what do you see that’s attractive here? ATUL: I think what Southwest has done is something that’s remarkable. They have gone about taking that — to your point earlier, when you talk about them being a model for, you know, the budget or the low-cost enterprise airlines. They have successfully, over a short period of time, added premium seating. They’ve also changed various other elements of the business model, like going from open seating policy to, you know, more assigned seating. They’ve changed some policy around bags, around a bunch of different things to make them more attractive to what the consumers want and desire now versus, you know, how they used to look at flying in the past. So they’ve gone through all these changes in a very short period of time. Their execution has been excellent, and we’re also seeing the results of the changes that they have made in their — in their P&L. So their margins are up meaningfully this year. So clearly, these changes are benefiting Southwest. And also, in the case of Delta, United, even Southwest, these are only really the three airlines that are meaningfully profitable this year, even in this fuel backdrop, and they’ve got strong balance sheets. The key reasons why we like all three of them. ANDREW: Before we let you go, I don’t know how new this is, but there’s a lot of investor attention being paid to the vast importance of credit cards for the airlines. Obviously, perks, etc., a way to attract customers. But airlines, for example, take in billions of dollars every year from the banks that run their credit cards. So the airlines are becoming more like banks. ATUL: Yes, and look, I mean, these credit cards and, you know, the loyalty piece that I was talking about earlier, they provide a good medium for these airlines to attract customers that are loyal and that continue to want to fly with that particular airline to which they are loyal. We think the loyalty, the revenues that are generating — these cards or the overall loyalty program — are higher-margin revenues than, you know, the base business of running an airline. And this has become increasingly important in the U.S. because if you have, you know, a strong base of these loyalty customers, you’re able to get that repeat business. You’re able to get, you know, the higher-margin revenues, and it kind of builds, you know, a flywheel for these airlines in their respective margins. So this is increasingly important, and I see it becoming even more important in the future. And the top airlines that have these — the Delta, United, the Southwest — they are going to benefit more and more as we — as we’ll see this play out over the next few years. ANDREW: Apparently, airlines are rushing to build ultra-luxe lounges around America to draw these credit card holders. I guess it’d be sitting on some anonymous bench in departures. Atul, thank you very much indeed for joining us. ATUL: Thank you for having me as well. ANDREW: Atul Maheswari, an equity analyst at UBS. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Oct. 14, 2026 interview with Atul Maheswari are published with the assistance of AI. Original research, interview questions and added context was created by BNN Bloomberg journalists. item.title: As Wall Street banks finance and adopt AI, risks mount on both fronts
item.description: Wall Street’s biggest banks want to ride the AI wave without getting caught in its undertow, as the promise of a lucrative infrastructure boom collides with questions over returns and new security ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Wall Street’s biggest banks want to ride the AI wave without getting caught in its undertow, as the promise of a lucrative infrastructure boom collides with questions over returns and new security threats. Executives at the largest U.S. banks this week discussed the risks of AI agents acting on customers’ behalf and the uncertainty surrounding demand for the capital and computing power needed to fuel the technology’s rapid growth. “While we are proud of the privileged position we play in the AI investment cycle, no one knows how the demands for capital and compute will evolve as the broader AI ecosystem matures,” Goldman CEO David Solomon said on a call with analysts. “That will only become clearer as technology and markets continue to develop. This uncertainty reinforces the importance of remaining vigilant around the types of activity we finance and how we manage risk.” Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser does not believe that higher rates will slow down the investment in the AI infrastructure. “We’re not seeing a slowdown in investment in the broader AI ecosystem. There’s simply not enough compute,” she said, referring to the processing power needed to develop and run AI models, supported by chips and data centers. Capital behind the great AI buildout The scale of investment in AI infrastructure is unprecedented. Big Tech has committed billions to building data centers, the backbone of the computing capacity needed to train and run generative AI models. For Wall Street, the buildout offers a chance to finance one of the biggest investment cycles in decades. Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said the enormous amount of AI capital investment is important for the lender’s investment-grade debt and leveraged finance businesses. Yet the financing opportunity hinges on several unknowns, from whether demand for computing power will keep pace with the industry’s ambitious expansion plans to the returns data center projects can generate and the potential for local opposition. “The AI investment cycle has become a complicated macroeconomic force in its own right,” Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf told analysts on a post-earnings call. He added that the buildout presents both opportunities and risks, given the significant leverage used to finance it and upward pressure on prices in some industries and supply chains. “Having said this, the strength of the economy and the positive forces from these investments have thus far outweighed the potential downside,” Scharf said. Elevated interest rates that stay higher for longer, or rise further, could increase financing costs for data center projects, squeeze returns and make it more expensive for borrowers to service debt. Morgan Stanley Chief Financial Officer Sharon Yeshaya said in an interview with Reuters that the bank was “very discerning” about the types of risks it was taking. “What you worry about is that peers and other firms allow for a loosening of credit standards, and that’s kind of what creates the issue. We’re very focused on making sure that we’re not involved in those types of transactions.” The bank’s CEO Ted Pick told analysts the involvement in AI financing is “existential” for Morgan Stanley. Investors, too, are weighing the economic benefits of the AI boom against the risk of losses on loans to projects that fail to deliver expected returns. “To the extent that the tech spend is helping drive growth in the overall economy, that is a positive and material to the banks. If the credit exposure is directly related to certain projects like speculative data-center builds, it could lead to issues down the road,” said Macrae Sykes, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, which holds several bank stocks. Other investors say that banks are better positioned to manage those risks than some fear, having tightened their risk management practices after the financial crisis. Dave Ellison, portfolio manager at Hennessy Funds, said banks have not abandoned the lessons of the crisis and are being more careful than investors fear. They are facilitating AI-related financing, but often as arrangers that distribute risk. Ringfencing emerging AI risks Beyond financing the buildout, banks are deploying AI in hopes of cutting costs and boosting productivity, but the financial payoff remains difficult to quantify. “As important and dramatic and exciting as this theme is, it takes a long time to really do things that are visible at an institution of our size,” JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said, adding that it is not a surprise that benefits are not yet observable in the bank’s quarterly earnings. Citi’s Fraser said the bank is already seeing clear effects of the use of AI, such as developing products at lower cost and up to 40% faster. The use of coding tools has eased development and reduced tech vendor expenses by 30%, she said. “We are seeing the financial benefits from AI and automation significantly outweigh the investments we’ve made year to date,” Fraser said. The bank is using AI to reduce the volume of manual processes, as well as response time in client service. Investors are betting on AI to deliver productivity gains across corporate America and valuations of US stocks leave little room for those gains to disappoint. “If those gains in productivity and lower costs do not arrive by the end of next year, investors will begin to question the hype of AI,” Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, said. At the same time, AI agents introduce new security challenges as they gain the ability to act autonomously. The technology is also adding to the threat posed by external cyber attackers. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said that the lender is developing tools to navigate agentic AI risk. (Reporting by Manya Saini in Bengaluru and Saeed Azhar and Tatiana Bautzer in New York; Editing by Aurora Ellis)
